# Skills {#sec-chapter-skills}

```{=typst}
#label("sec-chapter-skills")

// Rationale: Chapter opener at 80% width: an arcanist multi-tasking, showing the breadth of skills available to heroes in a single evocative image.
#image("assets/images/placeholder-ch07-skills.png", width: 80%)

_Figure 9.1: Skills_

#pagebreak()

Skills represent what your hero has learned to do. When the dice hit the table, your skill bonus is what separates "I tried" from "I succeeded." Every hero picks up skills in background and class training. The ones you invest in define how you solve problems: climbing a wall, reading a room, identifying a poison, or vanishing into a crowd.

Here is the core loop: the DA calls for a roll. You grab 3d6. You add the attribute the skill is keyed to. Then you add your skill bonus, +1 for Novice, +2 for Adept, +3 for Master. The DA grants a Boon or imposes a Bane for difficulty. Compare the total to the success tiers.

*Skills add +1/+2/+3 to rolls. Disciplines gate weapons, spells, and abilities; skills gate nothing.* If you want to swing a greatsword, you need the right weapon Disciplines, not a skill (see @sec-chapter-disciplines) A skill never unlocks a weapon, a spell, or an ability. It simply adds to a roll you are already allowed to make.

#pagebreak()

== Skill Tiers
#label("sec-skill-tiers")

Skills come in three tiers. Each tier raises your bonus on rolls made with that skill.

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (21.05%, 15.79%, 21.05%, 42.11%),
    align: (auto, auto, auto, auto,),
    table.header([Tier], [Bonus], [DP Cost], [Level Gate],),
    [*Novice*], [+1], [2 DP], [None (Level 1)],
    [*Adept*], [+2], [4 DP], [Level 3],
    [*Master*], [+3], [8 DP], [Level 7],
  )],
  caption: [Skill Tiers],
  kind: table,
  outlined: false,
  numbering: none,
)

All skills cost the same for every class: a Blade and an Arcanist pay the same for Novice Athletics, and either can learn any skill on the list. A class sheet's *Favored Skills* line is guidance on what that class does best, never a discount: the price above is the price. As with abilities, the higher tiers unlock as you level. Until a gate opens, everything you buy is Novice.

#pagebreak()

== How Skills Work in Play

When you attempt something with a meaningful chance of failure and consequence, the DA sets a difficulty and you roll. The total, 3d6 + attribute + skill, adjusted by any Boon or Bane, determines your success tier.

#figure(
  align(center)[#table(
    columns: (25%, 25%, 50%),
    align: (auto, auto, auto,),
    table.header([Success Tier], [Total], [What It Means],),
    [*Weak*], [1-8], [You succeed, but there's a cost, complication, or reduced effect.],
    [*Standard*], [9-14], [Clean success. You do the thing you set out to do.],
    [*Strong*], [15-18+], [Exceptional success. Extra effect, bonus information, or added style.],
    [*Critical*], [Three natural 6s], [Automatic Strong plus a special outcome.],
    [*Fumble*], [Three natural 1s], [Automatic failure with a serious complication.],
  )],
  caption: [Success Tiers in Play],
  kind: table,
  outlined: false,
  numbering: none,
)

*Totals of Zero or Less:* A final total of 0 or less is still Weak, and the DA adds one complication on top of it. The full tier rules, including the worked example for that case, live in @sec-chapter-core-resolution

*Difficulty.* The DA sets difficulty as a Boon, a Bane, or neither: favorable conditions grant a Boon, hostile conditions impose a Bane, and a fair task is a straight roll. A quality dwarven lock is harder than a squeaky door, and the Bane says so. The single Difficulty table, and how Boons and Banes stack and cancel, live in @sec-chapter-core-resolution

#callout(type: "note", title: "When NOT to Roll", body: [
If there's no consequence for failure and no pressure, don't roll dice. Just tell the story. The brawler with Brawn +2 wants to kick down a normal wooden door? It breaks. The woodsman with Survival Adept wants to find edible berries in a temperate forest? They find them. Rolling dice when there's nothing at stake drains tension from the moments that _do_ matter.

Roll when failure is interesting, when the outcome is uncertain, when the table is leaning forward to see what happens. Never roll just because the rules say there's a skill for it. The rules serve the story, not the other way around.
])

=== Worked Example: Skill in Action, Different Tiers, Different Outcomes

Makeva Quickfoot, a halfling Odd, is trying to pick the lock on a merchant's strongbox while the merchant is distracted at the front of the shop.

*The setup:* Makeva has Agility +1 and Thievery at Novice (+1). The lock is quality dwarven work and she's working fast, so the DA rules it Hard: a Bane. She rolls 4d6, keeps the lowest three, and adds 2 for Agility and skill.

Let's look at three possible outcomes:

*Result A, She rolls 4, 2, 3, 5 (keeps 2+3+4 = 9, +2 = 11, Standard):* The lock clicks open with a soft _snick._ She slips the strongbox open, pockets the ledger inside, and closes it again. The merchant hasn't noticed a thing. Clean. Professional.

*Result B, She rolls 4, 5, 6, 6 (keeps 4+5+6 = 15, +2 = 17, Strong):* The lock practically opens itself. Not only does she get the ledger, but she spots a false bottom in the strongbox, a pouch of uncut gems the merchant wasn't declaring to the tax collector. Bonus loot, and bonus leverage if she ever needs it.

*Result C, She rolls 1, 2, 2, 6 (keeps 1+2+2 = 5, +2 = 7, Weak):* She gets the ledger out, barely, but the lockpick snaps inside the mechanism, leaving a piece of metal visibly wedged in the lock. The DA makes a note: _the town guard will be asking questions tomorrow._

Same skill. Same Bane. Three different stories, all driven by the dice.

=== Worked Example: Skill vs Discipline

Kael, a dwarf Blade, wants to put a shortsword through a bandit captain. The shortsword is not a skill. It is a weapon, and weapons are gated by Disciplines. Kael has Melee, which the shortsword requires, so he may use it at all. His skill bonus does not enter the attack.

Now Kael wants to shove a heavy crate off a collapsing ledge to buy the party time. That is Athletics. Kael has Brawn +1 and Athletics at Novice (+1). The DA sets Hard: a Bane. He rolls 4d6, keeps the lowest three, and adds 2 for Brawn and Athletics. The +1 from Athletics makes the shove a little more likely to land, but it did not grant him permission to try. Any hero may attempt a skill. A Discipline decides whether you may use a weapon, spell, or ability at all.

== The 23 Skills
#label("sec-skill-list")

Twenty-three skills, grouped into five categories. Every skill shares the same three-tier bonus: Novice +1, Adept +2, Master +3. None of them have Discipline prerequisites, and none of them gate anything.

A few names do double duty in this book. *Parry* is a skill here and also a weapon maneuver (see @sec-chapter-combat) and *Stealth*, *Sleight*, *Lore* and *Religion* also name Disciplines (see @sec-chapter-disciplines) The distinction is what each one does: a skill adds to a roll you are already entitled to make, while a Discipline decides what you may attempt at all. The category headings below are organisational only; they are not Disciplines.

    [*Dodge*], [Agility], [Getting out of the way, diving clear, avoiding area effects],
    [*Parry*], [Brawn], [Blocking attacks with a weapon or shield; requires one in hand],
  )],
  caption: [Physical Skills],
  kind: table,
  outlined: false,
  numbering: none,
)

#callout(type: "note", title: "Shields and Parry", body: [
A shield enables Parry (it is an implement in hand) and Shield Block, but the shield itself never adds a bonus to the Parry roll. The only Parry roll bonus is the Parry skill rank; a shield's value arrives through Shield Block, as a Boon on the Defense Roll.
])

*Insight has two forms.* Rolled actively, it is keyed to Reason like any other skill. When someone is lying to you and you are not looking for it, you do not roll: the lie carries a Challenge set by your Knowledge modifier, negated (@sec-chapter-social-conflict)
```
